title: The Real Cost of Having Kids (No One Talks About This)
guest: Natasha Leggero (stand-up comedian, actress, author of 'The World Deserves My Children') and Sabrina Jalees (comedian, Emmy-nominated writer, co-hosts of the 'Good Enough' parenting podcast)
summary: The sisters, both childless, interview comedians Natasha Leggero and Sabrina Jalees about whether and when to have kids, fertility preservation, the true economics of babies, and how to pick a partner who will be a good parent. The guests argue that egg/embryo freezing removes the pressure to settle, that most baby spending (night nurses, new strollers) is unnecessary, and that parenting is the best 'next level' of life if you choose to frame it that way.

ideas.idea: You decide how you feel about getting older (and about parenting): if you plan on having a hard time, you will, and if you reframe it as accumulating wisdom and power, you won't.
ideas.detail: Sabrina's mother told her this when she worried that early teenage comedy success would make aging hard; Sabrina says this choice-of-frame is at the core of her parenting philosophy.

ideas.idea: Freeze eggs early and do two or three retrieval rounds, not one, because attrition from eggs to a live birth is brutal.
ideas.detail: Natasha froze 8 eggs at 38 for one hoped-for child; after thawing, fertilizing and genetic testing they went 8 to 4 to 2 to 1, so she had roughly a 30% chance of one baby from one round and could not afford a second. Cherie did two rounds.

ideas.idea: Freezing eggs rather than embryos is now nearly as successful and preserves optionality when you are not sure about your partner.
ideas.detail: Jean froze eggs while on the verge of an engagement that later ended; her doctor said improved freezing technology has narrowed the success gap between eggs and embryos, which she says 'saved her life' by not tying her to an ex.

ideas.idea: Fertility preservation relaxes the 'musical chairs' pressure on women in their late 30s and 40s so they do not settle into a bad relationship just to get the kid.
ideas.detail: Sabrina notes men do not face this predicament; Cherie says having her eggs frozen means she no longer feels pressure to find the right person right now. Egg freezing should be seen as a new timeline, not a concession.

ideas.idea: US fertility is at a historic low and the question has flipped from 'why wouldn't you have kids' to 'why would you'.
ideas.detail: The hosts cite the Congressional Budget Office projecting 1.58-1.63 births per woman as of 2026, after an all-time low of about 1.6 in 2024, and a stat that for the first time more US births are to women in their 40s than to teens.

ideas.idea: Anyone you respect who has kids will say it is the best part of their life; parenting is the next 'level' of the game where you shift from playing to shepherding.
ideas.detail: Sabrina admits the daunting cost of shelving your own needs, money and travel, but argues the rewards (a child teaching you 'God is hope plus love', people not addicted to phones) cannot be imagined by the childless.

ideas.idea: You don't get a 'bad kid'; whatever issues arise become the ride you are on, and how you handle them is your unique path through parenting.
ideas.detail: Sabrina says even behavioural issues are part of the journey, while acknowledging rare extreme cases; the core lesson is getting up after you fall down, the same trait that separates the graduates who 'make it'.

ideas.idea: If you struggle to like an aspect of your kid, it is really something you feel about yourself; your patience for them reflects your patience with yourself.
ideas.detail: Answering Jean's question about parents who secretly don't like their kids, Sabrina calls it inner-child work: kids are an extension of you, everyone should be in some therapy, and parents who outsource all parenting are the ones who end up disconnected.

ideas.idea: Use parenting as an opportunity to break perfectionist habits rather than fearing it will amplify them.
ideas.detail: Jean fears entering motherhood as an A+ student fixated on doing everything best. The guests cite Marie Kondo publicly abandoning her tidiness system after another child, and Sabrina's wife loosening her military-cleanliness upbringing because it is not sustainable with two kids.

ideas.idea: Talk openly about miscarriage: it is a common chromosomal outcome, especially when you wait longer, not a failure or a jinx.
ideas.detail: Sabrina lost a baby at 3.5 months after a failed IVF round and mentions it on every podcast because silence treats it like 'Bloody Mary'; she even objects to the word 'miscarriage' implying the mother messed up.

ideas.idea: Scheduling a C-section is a rational choice for the fear-driven or practical, but pregnancy itself can pull you into a 'motherhood Olympics' of wanting to do it naturally and perfectly.
ideas.detail: Natasha scheduled her C-section to avoid her water breaking in public; Sabrina, who pre-pregnancy thought any 1% safety edge justified a C-section, found herself wanting to be a 'bathtub lady' once pregnant.

ideas.idea: You do not need a night nurse; buy a second-hand Snoo instead and resell it when done.
ideas.detail: Everyone in Hollywood told Natasha she needed a night nurse; she paid one about $2,000 for a month, felt it was pointless since breastfeeding meant she woke anyway. The Snoo simulates womb sounds and motion and trains the baby to self-soothe; buying and reselling used (avoiding rented or fifth-hand units) can net out to near zero.

ideas.idea: Most baby gear cost is hype: buy second-hand, use Buy Nothing groups, and pass your stuff on when you outgrow it.
ideas.detail: Natasha bought a Doona stroller second-hand for $400 versus thousands new, comparing it to picking the $1 wedding chairs over $4 ones; Sabrina advocates an informal network where middle- and upper-class parents give gear away.

ideas.idea: Be present by structuring work around the school day: kids are gone 8 to 3 once in school, so aim to be home by 4.
ideas.detail: Advice Ali Wong gave Natasha: the first five years are hard, but afterwards you can build a career in school hours, be there mornings and from 4pm until the 6-7pm bedtime routine, then go out at night.

ideas.idea: Social algorithms scare each demographic into thinking they are doing parenting wrong; the guests started their podcast to discuss the imperfections.
ideas.detail: Just as the sisters' feeds show 'pregnancy nose' TikToks, parents' feeds say pack this lunch or never say that to your kid; Sabrina says treat any slip as a lesson rather than a catastrophe.

ideas.idea: Two kids is the sweet spot in a coastal city; three is too many pregnancies and too much competition for attention, and 'one is an accessory, two is a lifestyle'.
ideas.detail: Natasha (one child, born when she was 43) says a single child needs constant playdates, but three kids in LA is a step backwards for a career woman; if you live somewhere cheaper in the middle of the country, have five. Both sisters say they ideally want three.

ideas.idea: Don't let the dream of a child die because of the fertility bump or the partnership bump; solo parenting via donor or surrogate is a legitimate route.
ideas.detail: Sabrina cites Riki Lindhome, who had a child on her own, fulfilled her destiny without waiting for a man, and then fell in love with Fred Armisen. Both sisters say they want the full experience with a partner.

ideas.idea: Keep a list of negotiables and non-negotiables after each breakup; the non-negotiables grow and reveal why past relationships failed.
ideas.detail: Natasha's superficial wants (British, plays guitar) gave way to essentials: a partner who lets her shine, understands her drive, won't cheat (a roving eye 'eats you alive'), and genuinely wants kids, which is how she knew he'd be a good parent.

ideas.idea: The traits that make a good life partner, kindness and empathy that solve problems as a couple rather than fighting for one's own way, are the same traits that make a good co-parent.
ideas.detail: Sabrina says beauty is the first draft but kindness makes it sustainable; she knew her wife was 'the mother of my children' when she pulled out a giant box of art supplies on an early trip. People who think about others' experiences and adventures will do the same for a kid.

ideas.idea: Red flags do not change; if there are red flags, run.
ideas.detail: Sabrina initially said couples can 'get there together' over a long arc before kids, but reverses after noting Tiger Woods' drunk-driving pattern was a Chelsea Lately topic 15 years ago: 'patterns be patterns'.

ideas.idea: Endocrine disruptors (non-stick pans, scented candles) may explain earlier periods and are worth minimizing at home.
ideas.detail: Discussed when noting kids now start periods around 12; Sabrina's wife has thrown out such products and insists on wild over farmed fish, though Sabrina jokes ChatGPT told her farmed shrimp was fine.
